title: File System (fs)
subtitle: Reading, writing, and managing files with Node's fs module
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Real applications need to read configuration files, write logs, process data files, and manage uploads — file system access is fundamental to backend development.
whyItExists.solution: Node's built-in `fs` module provides synchronous and asynchronous APIs for all file system operations. The modern `fs/promises` (or `fs.promises`) API uses Promises/async-await for clean async code.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Reading config files, writing logs, serving static files, processing uploads, generating reports, data pipelines, scripts.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For web servers, let Express serve static files (it handles caching, ranges, MIME types). For large files, use streams instead of readFileSync (to avoid loading the whole file into memory).

explainModes.beginner: The fs module lets Node.js read and write files on the computer. `fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8')` reads a file and returns its content as a string. `fs.writeFileSync('output.txt', 'Hello')` creates or overwrites a file. For large files or many files at once, use the async version so your program doesn't freeze.
explainModes.simple: Three styles: Sync (readFileSync) — simple, blocks execution, fine for startup. Callback (readFile(path, cb)) — old-style async, error first: readFile(path, (err, data) => {}). Promise (fs.promises or import from 'fs/promises') — modern async. Use path.join() to build paths — never string concatenate paths. Always use 'utf8' encoding to get a string (default is Buffer). Check existence: fs.existsSync(path).
explainModes.standard: Common operations: readFileSync/readFile, writeFileSync/writeFile, appendFileSync/appendFile, mkdirSync/mkdir ({recursive: true}), readdirSync/readdir, statSync/stat, unlinkSync/unlink (delete), renameSync/rename (move). JSON pattern: JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('data.json', 'utf8')). Error handling: ENOENT (file not found), EACCES (permission denied), EEXIST (directory already exists). Streams: for files > few MB, use createReadStream/createWriteStream to process in chunks.
explainModes.technical: fs.stat vs fs.exists: stat gives you metadata (size, mtime, isFile, isDirectory); it throws ENOENT if not found. existsSync just returns boolean. The stat/existsSync race condition: between checking and using, the file can disappear. Handle errors from the read/write operations directly instead. File descriptors: openSync/open gives you an fd (integer) for lower-level read/write operations. Useful for random access (seeking) or writing large files. Watching files: fs.watch(path, callback) — notifies on changes. Used by Node --watch, chokidar, and build tools.
explainModes.deepDive: The thread pool: fs operations (except statSync, existsSync, readdirSync, fstatSync) run in libuv's thread pool. The pool has 4 threads by default (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4). If your app does many concurrent fs.readFile calls, they queue behind pool threads. For heavy parallel file I/O, increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Streams: createReadStream returns a Readable stream. Pipe to a Writable: readStream.pipe(writeStream). In Node 18+, use stream/promises and pipeline for async/await friendly streaming. OPFS (Origin-Private File System): in the browser, you can't use Node fs — OPFS is the modern browser equivalent for persistent file storage.

questions.question: Why should you use `fs.readFile` (async) instead of `fs.readFileSync` in a web server?
options: readFileSync is deprecated — you must use readFile
readFileSync blocks the event loop while the file reads; in a server, this blocks ALL other requests from being handled during that time
readFile is always faster than readFileSync
readFileSync only works for small files
questions.explanation: readFileSync blocks the entire Node.js event loop — while it's reading the file, no other code can run. In a web server, this means no other requests are handled during that disk I/O. readFile (async) offloads the I/O to libuv's thread pool and returns immediately — the event loop can handle other requests while the file is being read, then calls back when done. readFileSync is fine for startup code (config loading) but dangerous in request handlers.

faq.q: How do I read a JSON file in Node.js?
faq.a: Two ways: (1) fs: `const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('data.json', 'utf8'))` — always specify 'utf8' encoding. (2) In Node 20+ with `"type": "module"`, you can use `import data from './data.json' assert { type: 'json' }`. The fs approach works in both CJS and ESM and is more explicit.

examples: const config = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('config.json', 'utf8')) — load app config
await fs.promises.writeFile('output.csv', csvData) — save processed data
